entry: American multinational retail corporation headquartered in Bentonville, [[Arkansas]]. It operates hypermarkets (also called supercenters), discount department stores, grocery stores, pharmacies and gas stations in the United States and 19 other countries, and owns the Sam's Club warehouse clubs. Brothers [[Sam Walton]] and James "Bud" Walton founded it in 1962 in Rogers, Arkansas. It was listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] in 1972 and moved to the [[Nasdaq]] in December 2025. By 1988 it was the most profitable retailer in the United States, and by October 1989 the largest by revenue. The Walton family controls the company, and Sam Walton's heirs own over 50 percent of it, making it the largest family-owned public business in the world. In February 2026 it became the first traditional retailer valued at over $1 trillion. It employs 2.1 million people and is the largest private employer in the world. Unions and advocacy groups criticize its wages and labor practices; the company cites entry-level opportunities and recent wage increases.

Edible [[Seed|seed]] of any tree of the genus *Juglans*, most often the Persian or English walnut, *J. regia*. After ripening, the shell is discarded and the kernel eaten. Walnuts ripen between September and November in the northern hemisphere. The antioxidants in the brown seed coat protect the oil-rich kernel from atmospheric oxygen, preventing rancidity. Hulls contain polyphenols that stain hands and can irritate the skin, and juglone reached 2–4% of fresh weight in the husks. The Persian walnut, which originated in Iran, is the species most often grown, and nearly all cultivars are hybrids of it. The element *wal* in the name is Germanic and means foreign, as in [[Wales]] and [[Wallachia]]. Poor storage lets molds produce aflatoxin, a potent [[Carcinogen|carcinogen]]; walnuts keep best below 25 °C (77 °F) in low humidity.

Large [[Pinniped|pinniped]] marine mammal with prominent tusks and whiskers, *Odobenus rosmarus*. It is the only living species in the family Odobenidae. Walruses range across the Arctic Ocean and subarctic seas of the Northern Hemisphere, in two subspecies, the Atlantic and the Pacific. Adult Pacific males can weigh more than 2,000 kilograms (4,400 pounds), and among pinnipeds only the two elephant seal species exceed them in size. They live mostly in shallow water over the [[Continental shelf|continental shelves]], feeding on benthic bivalve molluscs and often resting on [[Sea ice|sea ice]]. Considered a keystone species of the Arctic marine region, the walrus figures prominently in the cultures of Indigenous Arctic peoples. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, commercial hunting for blubber, ivory, leather and meat sharply reduced populations. They have partly recovered, but Atlantic and Laptev populations remain fragmented and low. The IUCN lists the species as Vulnerable, citing sea ice loss linked to Arctic warming.

Entertainment and vacation resort complex about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of [[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]], opened October 1, 1971, and operated by Disney Experiences of the [[The Walt Disney Company|Walt Disney Company]]. Covering about 27,000 acres, it has four theme parks, two water parks, four golf courses and 31 Disney-owned resort hotels. Conceived as a supplement to [[Disneyland]] in [[Anaheim, California|Anaheim]], it was planned by [[Walt Disney]] and built after his death. In 2024 it was the most visited vacation resort in the world, with average annual attendance of more than 49 million.

American poet, essayist and journalist, often called the father of free verse. He combined [[Transcendentalism|transcendentalism]] with realism in writing that was controversial in his time. His major work, *Leaves of Grass*, was first published in 1855, financed with his own money, and was revised until his death; some called it obscene for its overt sensuality. Raised in [[Brooklyn]], he left formal schooling at age 11 and later worked as a printer, journalist, teacher and government clerk. During the [[American Civil War]] he went to [[Washington, D.C.]], where he nursed the wounded in hospitals. After the [[Assassination of Abraham Lincoln|assassination]] of Abraham Lincoln, whom he greatly admired, he wrote poems including "O Captain! My Captain!" A [[Stroke|stroke]] late in life left his health in decline, and he moved to Camden, New Jersey. [[Ezra Pound]] called him "America's poet."

American broadcast journalist, anchorman of the [[CBS]] Evening News from 1962 to 1981. He reported on events from 1937 to 1981, including World War II bombings, the [[Nuremberg trials]], combat in the [[Vietnam War]] and the [[Iran hostage crisis]]. Often cited in the 1960s and 1970s as "the most trusted man in America" after an opinion poll, he received two Peabody Awards and the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He covered the space program from Project Mercury to the Moon landings and the [[Space Shuttle]]. He closed broadcasts with the phrase "And that's the way it is." After the [[Tet Offensive]], his February 27, 1968, special report called the war "mired in stalemate," a conclusion that reportedly influenced President [[Lyndon B. Johnson]]'s decision not to seek re-election. Some praised the report for its candor; critics argued it reflected liberal bias.

German-American architect and founder of the [[Bauhaus]] school in Weimar. He is regarded as one of the pioneering masters of modernist architecture and became a leading proponent of the International Style. He taught at the Bauhaus for several years and led it until 1928. Gropius emigrated to England in 1934 and to the United States in 1937, where he taught at the [[Harvard University|Harvard Graduate School of Design]]. In America he worked with Marcel Breuer and co-founded The Architects Collaborative. His early works include the Faguswerk shoe-last factory in Alfeld-an-der-Leine, Germany, whose glass curtain walls (1911) anticipated modernism. He also designed an office and factory building for the 1914 Werkbund Exhibition in [[Cologne]]. Having established a practice in [[Berlin]] in 1910, he won the AIA Gold Medal in 1959.

American journalist and media critic. With a career spanning 60 years, he was among the first to introduce the concept of the [[Cold War]] and coined the term "[[Stereotype|stereotype]]" in its modern psychological sense. His 1922 *Public Opinion* critiqued media and democracy, and James W. Carey called it "the founding book of modern journalism." He was research director of [[Woodrow Wilson]]'s board of inquiry after [[World War I]], and his views on journalism were contrasted with those of [[John Dewey]] in the Lippmann–Dewey Debate. He won two [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prizes]], one for his syndicated column "Today and Tomorrow" and one for an interview with [[Nikita Khrushchev]]. He has been called the "Father of Modern Journalism."

American actor known for his "hangdog face" and world-weary characters. He starred in 10 films with his friend [[Jack Lemmon]], including *The Odd Couple* (1968). On Broadway he originated the role of Oscar Madison in Neil Simon's *The Odd Couple*, winning a Tony Award in 1965. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *The Fortune Cookie* (1966), directed by [[Billy Wilder]], and is also known for *Charade* (1963) and *The Bad News Bears* (1976). In 1982 he received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American professional football running back, nicknamed "Sweetness." He played 13 seasons with the [[Chicago]] Bears of the [[National Football League]], who selected him fourth overall in the 1975 draft. He won the 1977 AP NFL Most Valuable Player Award and [[Super Bowl|Super Bowl XX]] with the 1985 Bears, and was a nine-time Pro Bowl selection. At retirement he held the NFL career rushing record, with 16,726 yards. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1993. His legacy includes the Walter Payton Man of the Year Award.

Scottish novelist, poet and historian, known for the Waverley novels. Published between 1814 and 1831, the Waverley novels were for nearly a century among the most popular and widely read novels in Europe. He also wrote narrative poems including *Marmion* (1808) and *The Lady of the Lake* (1810), and his historical novels helped establish the genre as an exemplar of European [[Romanticism]]. Born in [[Edinburgh]], he was left lame by a childhood bout of [[Polio|polio]] in 1773. He worked as an advocate and legal administrator, and was created a baronet in 1820. In 1822 he orchestrated the visit of [[George IV|King George IV]] to Scotland, reviving interest in Highland tartans and clan traditions. After a financial crisis in 1826 linked to the failed Ballantyne printing firm, he refused bankruptcy and repaid creditors through his writing.

[[Ballroom dance|Ballroom]] and [[Folk dance|folk]] dance in triple (3/4) time, performed mainly in closed position. It originated in German-speaking Europe in the 18th century, when lower-class couples in [[Bavaria]], Tyrol and Styria began dancing a couple's dance called *Walzer* around 1750. The waltz became fashionable in [[Vienna]] around the 1780s, where its tempo was sped up. It reportedly reached England in 1791, and during the [[Napoleonic Wars]] soldiers of the King's German Legion introduced it to Bexhill, Sussex, from 1804. It became fashionable in Britain during the Regency period. Almack's, London's most exclusive club, permitted it, though the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] shows it was considered "riotous and indecent" as late as 1825. Composers of the Strauss family elevated it in orchestral works.

Chinese poet, painter, musician and statesman of the middle [[Tang dynasty]]. He is regarded as one of the most distinguished figures in Chinese arts and letters, renowned for his dual talents as a nature poet and landscape painter. About 400 of his poems survived, and 29 are included in the 18th-century anthology *Three Hundred Tang Poems*. No authenticated paintings survive, and none of his music is preserved. Born into an aristocratic family, he passed the palace examination in 721 with top place and first served as a court musician. He was demoted to overseeing a granary in the former province of Jizhou, now in [[Hebei]]. Later he was posted to the frontier at Liangzhou. Late in life he became a devout Chan Buddhist and a vegetarian. His poems were compiled at imperial command by his brother Wang Jin.

Chinese politician, general and calligrapher of the [[Jin dynasty (266–420)|Jin dynasty]], often regarded as the greatest calligrapher in Chinese history. Born in Langya Commandery, in present-day Linyi, [[Shandong]], he fled south in childhood after the collapse of the Western Jin dynasty. He received the title General of the Right Army in 347 and was appointed administrator of Kuaiji. In 353 he hosted a gathering at the Orchid Pavilion, where he composed the preface *Lantingji xu*, his most famous work. He retired from government in 355 to practice Taoism. He was proficient in the regular, semi-cursive and cursive scripts, but no original works survive, only rubbings and tracing copies. [[Emperor Taizong of Tang]] established his style as the standard for [[Calligraphy]] by requiring court scholars to study it, and Wang was posthumously titled the "Sage of Calligraphy."

Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher of the [[Ming dynasty]]. After [[Zhu Xi]], he is commonly regarded as the most important Neo-Confucian thinker. His interpretations rejected the rationalist dualism of Zhu Xi's orthodoxy, and with Lu Xiangshan he founded the Lu–Wang school, or School of the [[Mind]]. He held that the mind itself is principle and that knowledge and action are unified. Exiled to Guizhou in 1507 for protesting eunuch influence at court, he reached an intellectual breakthrough the following year. Reinstated, he suppressed peasant uprisings and princely rebellions, including the 1519 Ning Wang revolt. He is known by his honorific name in China, Japan and the West, and his ideas influenced Japanese Oyomeigaku.

Internal combustion engine using an eccentric rotary design, in which a rotor turns inside a figure-eight-like housing to convert pressure into rotating motion. German engineer Felix Wankel proved the concept, and German engineer Hanns-Dieter Paschke designed the first commercially feasible engine. Basic gasoline versions have lower thermal efficiency and higher exhaust emissions than four-stroke piston engines, which has restricted their use. Its compact size, smoothness and few parts suit [[Chainsaw|chainsaws]], [[Motorcycle|motorcycles]], [[Aircraft|aircraft]] and [[Unmanned aerial vehicle|unmanned aerial vehicles]]. [[Mazda]] produced the first production vehicle with one, the 1967 Cosmo Sport.

Emperor of the [[Ming dynasty]] of China, reigning from 1572 to 1620. He succeeded his father, the Longqing Emperor, at the age of nine. During the first ten years of his reign, Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng effectively led the government, and the country enjoyed economic and military prosperity. After Zhang died in 1582, the emperor increasingly withdrew from governance, at times holding no court audiences for more than two decades. A succession dispute over his favored third son, Zhu Changxun, pitted him against officials who backed his eldest son, Zhu Changluo, and lasted more than 15 years. He committed over 100,000 troops to support Korea against the Japanese invasions led by [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] in the [[Imjin War]]. In 1619 Jurchen forces defeated the Ming at the Battle of Sarhu. Zhu Changluo succeeded him as the Taichang Emperor in 1620.

Epic [[Novel|novel]] by [[Leo Tolstoy]], set during the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. An early version, *The Year 1805*, was serialized in *The Russian Messenger* from 1865 to 1867 before the complete novel appeared in 1869. It uses five interlocking narratives of Russian aristocratic families to illustrate [[Napoleon]]'s impact on Tsarist society, chronicling the French invasion of Russia and the [[Battle of Austerlitz]]. Large sections are philosophical discussions. Tolstoy argued that great events arise from the collective actions of multitudes rather than the will of leaders, critiquing deterministic [[Historiography|historiography]]. Regarded with [[Anna Karenina]] as Tolstoy's finest achievement, it is a classic of world literature, widely translated and adapted into films, operas and television series.

Serious violation of the laws of armed conflict that gives rise to individual criminal responsibility under international law. Examples include intentionally killing civilians, [[Torture|torture]], taking hostages, unnecessarily destroying civilian property, perfidy, pillaging and conscripting children into the military. Ordering mass killings, including [[Genocide|genocide]], is also a war crime. The concept emerged from the 1863 Lieber Code of the Union Army in the [[American Civil War]] and from the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907. After [[World War II]], trials of Axis leaders at [[Nuremberg trials|Nuremberg]] and [[Tokyo]] established that international criminal law defines war crimes. The 1998 Rome Statute established the [[International Criminal Court]], which defines more than 50 war crimes, though its jurisdiction is limited by state consent and Security Council referrals.

Elephant trained and equipped for use in combat. War elephants served as living siege engines, platforms for archers and terror weapons that could break enemy lines. The practice began in ancient India during the [[Vedic period]]. Alexander the Great's army met them in 326 BCE at the Battle of the Hydaspes. [[Carthage]] employed African forest elephants, and [[Hannibal]] took 37 of them across the [[Alps]] in 218 BCE to invade Italy. The [[Roman Republic]] later viewed them as novelties after defeats by [[Pyrrhus of Epirus]]. War elephants remained in Southeast Asian armies until gunpowder weapons replaced them. Each needed up to 300 pounds of fodder daily, and wounded elephants could stampede and endanger their own side.

Armed conflict in Afghanistan, begun as a U.S.-led invasion after the [[September 11 attacks]]. The [[Taliban]] refused to extradite [[Osama bin Laden]] and were expelled from major cities, but regrouped into an insurgency. Coalition forces peaked at about 140,000 in 2011, the year a U.S. raid killed bin Laden in Pakistan. After a 2020 agreement with the United States, the Taliban retook [[Kabul]] on August 15, 2021. It was the longest war in U.S. history, surpassing the [[Vietnam War]] by seven months, and killed an estimated 176,000–212,000+ people, including 46,319 civilians.

Conflict between the [[United States]] and the United Kingdom, fought mainly in North America and at sea, 1812–1815. The United States objected to British restrictions on trade with Napoleonic France and to the [[Royal Navy]]'s impressment of seamen. It declared war on June 18, 1812, with the [[Democratic-Republican Party]] in favor and the [[Federalist Party]] opposed. American invasions of Canada failed, and in August 1814 British forces captured and burned Washington. The Treaty of [[Ghent]] restored pre-war territory without settling the maritime issues. Andrew Jackson's army repulsed a British attack on [[New Orleans]] in January 1815, after the treaty had been signed.

Conflict among the European great powers, 1740–1748, fought mainly in Europe and on the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Its immediate cause was the right of [[Maria Theresa]] to inherit Austria. A coalition of France, Prussia and Bavaria challenged her inheritance, while [[Great Britain]], the Dutch Republic and Hanover backed her. Prussia began the fighting by occupying the wealthy Austrian province of [[Silesia]] in December 1740. The conflict later drew in [[Saxony]], Spain, Sweden and Russia. By early 1748 France was close to bankruptcy from the cost of the war and a British naval blockade. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle confirmed Maria Theresa in her titles, but Britain's insistence that Austria cede Silesia to [[Prussia]] undermined the Anglo-Austrian alliance. This led to the Diplomatic Revolution and, in 1756, the [[Seven Years' War]].

Phase of the [[Napoleonic Wars]], 1806–1807, in which a coalition whose main members were Prussia and Russia was defeated by France. Napoleon crushed the Prussians at Jena and Auerstedt in October 1806 and captured [[Berlin]]. The inconclusive battle of Eylau in February 1807 was followed by a French victory at Friedland in June. The Treaties of Tilsit (July 1807) made Russia join the Continental System and stripped Prussia of territory west of the [[Elbe]] and in the former [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]]. Napoleon then controlled most of western and central continental Europe, though Britain remained at war with France.

Territorial conflict between [[Chile]] and allied [[Peru]] and [[Bolivia]], 1879–1884. It was fought over [[Nitrate|nitrate]]-rich territory in the [[Atacama Desert]], as [[Guano|guano]] supplies declined. Bolivia taxed a Chilean-operated nitrate company in violation of an 1874 treaty, and Chile occupied the Bolivian port of Antofagasta in February 1879. Peru had a secret alliance with Bolivia. Chile won at sea and on land, capturing [[Lima]] in January 1881. Bolivia withdrew after the Battle of Tacna in May 1880, leaving Peru to fight on alone. The Treaty of Ancón (October 1883) gave Chile Peru's Tarapacá region and temporary control of Tacna and Arica. A 1904 treaty with Bolivia fixed the boundaries, leaving Bolivia landlocked.
